name: Cocoa butter / shea / coconut oil
lead: Cocoa butter, shea butter and coconut oil are plant fats widely used in moisturizers, soaps and lotions, and are a traditional folk choice for trying to prevent stretch marks in pregnancy.[1][2][3] They are applied to soften dry or ashy skin, to give the skin a smoother, more even surface, and, by lifters and some looksmaxxing forum users, over areas prone to stretch marks such as the shoulders, chest and thighs.[8][9]

Coconut oil is also used on hair and, by some forum users, on eyebrows. Looksmax.org guides describe coconut oil as a pre-wash or post-wash hair treatment for frizzy or damaged hair, and a forum post describes using it with argan oil on eyebrows.[10][11][12]

On the research side, a Cochrane review summarized on Wikipedia found no evidence that creams or oils prevent or reduce stretch marks in pregnancy.[4] A registered randomized trial of cocoa butter for stretch marks in pregnancy exists.[5] Reviews of topical plant oils describe barrier-repair and moisturizing properties for several oils, including coconut oil and shea butter.[6][7]

paras: Cocoa butter is mostly triglycerides of palmitic, oleic and stearic acids and melts near body temperature; it is common in lotions and soaps for its emollient feel.[1] Shea butter is a triglyceride fat rich in stearic and oleic acids, used as an emollient and skin conditioner.[2] Coconut oil is about 82% saturated fat, mostly lauric acid, and is a raw material in soaps and surfactants.[3]

Reviews of natural oils for skin describe them as accessible, inexpensive topical options, and note that oils differ in their fatty acid ratios, which are described as major determinants of barrier-repair effects. One review says oils with a higher linoleic-to-oleic acid ratio have better barrier-repair potential, while oils higher in oleic acid may be detrimental to barrier function.[7] A separate review covers anti-inflammatory and barrier-repair effects of topical plant oils including coconut oil and shea butter.[6]

Cocoa use traces back to the Aztecs and ancient Maya. The fat was first separated by boiling cocoa mass in water and skimming it, hydraulic presses were used from the 18th century, and the Van Houten press came into use in the second half of the 19th century. Until the late 19th century cocoa butter was largely a by-product of chocolate making, used mainly in cosmetic and pharmaceutical preparations, before becoming a standard chocolate ingredient.[1]

Cocoa butter is valued in skin products for what Wikipedia describes as a velvety texture, pleasant scent and emollient properties, and it stays stable near body temperature with a shelf life of roughly two to five years. Cheaper fats such as coconut, palm, shea and mango kernel fat are sometimes substituted for it commercially.[1]

Shea butter is extracted from the nut of the African shea tree (Vitellaria paradoxa), which grows wild across the dry savannah belt of West Africa. Traditional preparation is done by hand, production is documented by the 14th century, and the butter was being imported into Britain by 1846. The raw fat is ivory-coloured and mainly composed of oleic and stearic acids, with composition varying by region; it is used in cooking in some African countries and mainly in the cosmetics industry elsewhere as an emollient and skin conditioner.[2]

Coconut oil is a saturated vegetable fat obtained from the coconut and used in cooking, soap-making and cosmetics. In the hair and skin communities that discuss it online, it is treated as a low-cost, widely available emollient.[3][10]

A 2004 randomized double-blind trial compared extra virgin coconut oil with mineral oil as a moisturizer for mild to moderate xerosis (dry skin).[13] Forum users on T Nation describe cocoa butter for winter 'ashy' skin, although one writer noted that most lotions gave him acne.[14]

Stretch marks form when the dermis tears during rapid growth or stretching, as in puberty, pregnancy, weight gain or muscle gain, and they usually fade but do not disappear completely.[4] On T Nation, lifters describe applying cocoa butter to shoulders, chest and thighs where growth is fast, and one member wrote that cocoa butter and shea butter creams are 'supposed to help'.[8][9] Others in the same discussions say the cream did little for them.[15]

Looksmax.org guides promote coconut oil as a protective pre-wash coating for frizzy or damaged hair, and note it is not intended as a remedy for androgenetic alopecia.[10][11] One forum post describes alternating argan and coconut oil on eyebrows for two weeks and reports longer, thicker brows; other users in the thread suggest castor oil may be better.[12]

Wikipedia's stretch marks article reports that a Cochrane systematic review found no evidence that creams or oils prevent or reduce stretch marks in pregnancy, and that no treatment is clearly effective once marks have formed; tretinoin 0.1 percent was effective on early marks in several studies.[4] The article does not discuss cocoa butter specifically.[4]

For skin dryness, reviews of topical plant oils describe moisturizing and barrier effects for several oils.[6][7] Research on coconut oil in diet (for example a 2018 randomized trial comparing coconut oil, olive oil and butter on blood lipids) concerns eating it, not applying it.[16]

Wikipedia's account of the Cochrane review notes that the evidence addressed creams and oils as a group in pregnancy; it does not isolate cocoa butter, shea butter or coconut oil individually.[4] Supporters of these fats for stretch marks frame them as a way to keep skin supple while the dermis is under tension, a reasoning stated by forum users in lifting communities rather than tested in published trials.[8][9]

No specific harms of topical cocoa butter, shea butter or coconut oil have been described; as with any topical product, individual skin reactions are possible. Forum users have reported that some lotions and heavier moisturizers gave them acne.[14] Coconut oil is high in saturated fat when eaten, and nutrition reviews discuss its effect on blood lipids.[16]

Coconut oil, shea and cocoa butter are heavy, oil-rich products, and users in forums describe some as feeling greasy or triggering breakouts on acne-prone skin.[14] Reviews of natural oils for skin note that oils differ in fatty acid profile and that oils higher in oleic acid may be detrimental to barrier function, which is why oil choice is discussed in the dermatology literature.[7]

A registered randomized trial, "Cocoa Butter for Prevention of Stretch Marks" (200 participants, pregnancy, started 2004, completed), is listed on ClinicalTrials.gov.[5] Its results are not reproduced here. Broader reviews summarized on Wikipedia report no evidence that creams or oils prevent stretch marks.[4] A 2004 randomized double-blind trial compared extra virgin coconut oil with mineral oil for mild to moderate xerosis.[13] No trials of shea butter or coconut oil for stretch marks were found.

lore.intro: These fats are mentioned in lifting and looksmaxxing forums as stretch-mark prevention, as skin conditioners and, for coconut oil, as hair and brow treatments.[8][9][10][12]

claims.claim: Cocoa butter, shea or coconut oil prevents stretch marks
claims.believers: Lifters and pregnancy-care circles apply them to areas of fast growth. One T Nation member says he applies cocoa butter to his legs to 'mitigate stretch marks', and another says shea- and cocoa-butter creams are 'supposed to help'.[8][9]
claims.experts: A Cochrane review summarized on Wikipedia found no evidence that creams or oils prevent or reduce stretch marks in pregnancy.[4]

claims.claim: Cocoa butter did nothing for my stretch marks
claims.believers: A T Nation member who used cocoa butter pregnancy cream with a roommate says he never thought it did anything.[15]
claims.experts: Review evidence similarly reports no effect of creams or oils on stretch marks in pregnancy.[4]

claims.claim: Coconut oil improves frizzy or damaged hair
claims.believers: A looksmax.org guide says coconut oil reduces frizz and restores shine, citing a study on protein loss; users describe applying it before washing.[10][11]
claims.experts: The guide's own reference is not among the studies reviewed here; reviews on topical plant oils concern skin barrier repair.[6][7]

claims.claim: Argan or coconut oil makes eyebrows grow longer
claims.believers: One looksmax.org user reports eyebrows nearly doubling in length in two weeks and suggests castor oil may be best.[12]
claims.experts: No published study of coconut oil for eyebrow growth was found.

card.summary: Folk stretch mark moisturizers; reviews found no evidence they prevent marks.
card.note: Used as moisturizers; stretch mark prevention not shown.

quick.overview:
These plant fats are common moisturizing ingredients and a traditional choice for preventing stretch marks.
A registered trial of cocoa butter exists, but reviews summarized on Wikipedia report no evidence that creams or oils prevent stretch marks.
quick.mechanism: They act as emollients that soften and hydrate the skin surface; no mechanism for preventing stretch marks is established.
quick.risks: No specific harms are described; individual skin reactions to any topical product are possible.

chain: Fat-based emollient coats and softens the skin surface
Skin looks smoother and less dry or ashy
Used on areas prone to stretch marks in hope of fewer or fainter marks
angle.text: People rub these butters and oils into the skin to moisturize it and to reduce dryness or flaking, and some apply them to growth areas hoping to keep stretch marks from showing. The moisturizing effect is visible on the skin surface; the stretch mark benefit is what proponents expect rather than what trials have shown.
